Survey discrimination 43% over 5 years, highest among trans — that's everyday exposure. Elevated band. ~0.52.

Dossier 5 has more protections actually operating plus higher acceptance; but documented recurring unremedied custodial violations (tier 1). Dossier 4 also has prison unresolved plus higher official hostility and discrimination prevalence at scale. Hmm.

Dossier 5: 64% trans report identity-related discrimination (2023 survey) — primary everyday exposure per rule 21. Dossier 4: 43% discriminated/harassed in past 5 years, highest among trans; 51% targeted by insults/assault/threats. Dossier 4 also has head-of-state hostility, rising anti-LGBT political speech 71%, constitutional ban on same-sex marriage with 80-90% seats. Dossier 5 has official institutions working for trans people (ombudsman, custodial inspector with binding guidance, parliament scrutiny, hate crime enforcement), high public acceptance (84% equal rights). Dossier 4's institutions are partly working too (constitutional court, supreme court, hate crime prosecutions), but politicians hostile.

I'd put Dossier 5 slightly above Dossier 4: D5 ~0.55, D4 ~0.50. Actually D5's custodial violations are persistent and unremedied with a documented border incident too. D5's protections are stronger and society more accepting. Rule 11: strong rule of law discounts hostility where courts work for trans people — in D5 courts/ombudsman do work for trans people partially (binding guidance) though practice unchanged. In D4 courts struck down sterilization, supreme court rebuked lower court — also working.

I'll go D4 0.50, D5 0.56.

Dossier 1: 0.10. Active criminalization, mass arrests of trans women under morality provisions, forced anal exams (though those target gay men), systemic identity refusal, prison by birth gender, no protections. Not organized campaign with executions, so not 0.0. 0.10-0.12.

Dossier 2: 0.82. Strong protections, marriage equality, admin LGR, but prison placement imperfections, 2025 rollback of sex ed, UN concerns about discrimination. Also historical 1990 visa policy on unaccompanied women (dated). Low risk band: 0.83.

No documented trans-specific violence, no documented visitor-facing state restriction. Discrimination/harassment in healthcare documented for residents. Youth survey 58% accept LGBTQ family members. Rule 13: latent tangential statute + open questions + thin formal recourse = a step below acceptance-with-protections tier. No trans-specific acceptance tradition documented but visible tolerant social scene (pride 28k, gay bars, travel operator friendly). Open question on border treatment. I'd say 0.66.

Ranking: 2 > 3 > 5 > 4 > 1. Reasonable.

Rule: tier-1 worst feature rates materially below tier-3. D3's worst feature: paper protections not operating / media regulation / facility friction (tier 3-5). D5's worst is tier 1. Hmm, but D5 also has documented discrimination prevalence at scale (64%) — rule 21 says that puts in Elevated band even without criminal statute. D5 at 0.56 is elevated band. D3 at 0.66 reduced band. That ordering seems consistent with the precedence ladder (tier 1 below tier 3). But D3's tier... is D3 really tier 3? Its worst is "societal disapproval with thin recourse" — gender identity not in workplace law, no org registration — paper protections. So D3 above D5. Fine.

Wait — should D5 be lower given tier 1? The band implication says universal-exposure practices without working remedy sit in Elevated Risk. D5 is 0.56 — elevated. OK.

Final: 1: 0.10, 2: 0.83, 3: 0.66, 4: 0.50, 5: 0.56.
